summary: Some Network Time Protocol modes need a well-known local port, but others do not, and using it anyway makes blind off-path attacks easier. This document updates RFC 5905 to recommend ephemeral port randomization for modes where the well-known port is not required.

plainLanguage.summary: If the door you always use is easy to guess, a sneaky person can try knocking on it. This document says to use a random door when no fixed door is needed for clock messages.

questions: which ntp modes use a random source port
subtitle: Why NTP clients should stop using port 123 as their own source port, and pick a random one instead.

tldr.problem: Many NTP clients send requests from the well-known port 123 or from predictable ports, which gives blind off-path attackers one less thing to guess.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9109 rewrites the dstport description in RFC 5905 so that client mode (3) SHOULD use a randomized port as in RFC 6056, while broadcast server mode (5) and symmetric modes (1 and 2) keep port 123.
tldr.outcome: Client-side NTP becomes harder to attack with forged packets, at the cost of some effects on path selection that implementations must weigh.

today: RFC 9109 is a Proposed Standard from August 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it updates RFC 5905.

sections.title: The Problem with a Fixed Port
sections.content:
The Network Time Protocol (NTP) can run in several modes. Some modes must receive unsolicited packets, so they need the NTP well-known port, 123. Other modes do not, yet implementations often use port 123 as their local port anyway.

Several NTP attacks are blind or off-path: the attacker cannot see the traffic but sends forged packets to one or both peers. Many of them need the attacker to guess the NTP association, identified by the tuple {srcaddr, srcport, dstaddr, dstport, keyid}. A fixed port removes one unknown from that guess.

The RFC cites a study of NTP clients that found many use port 123 as the local port or choose predictable ephemeral ports. BCP 156 (RFC 6056) already recommends randomizing ephemeral ports. This document brings NTP in line by updating RFC 5905.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a secret club where everyone always knocks on door number 123. Anyone can guess it. If each visitor picks a random door, outsiders have a much harder time guessing.

sections.title: Port Randomization Against Off-Path Attacks
sections.content:
To attack a transport or upper-layer protocol instance blindly, an attacker must know or guess the five-tuple {Protocol, IP Source Address, IP Destination Address, Source Port, Destination Port}. Making that five-tuple harder to guess helps against such attacks.

The RFC presents ephemeral port randomization as a transport-layer mitigation. It does not replace other defences at other layers, and those do not replace it. The text notes that some other mitigations may be ineffective against certain off-path attacks, or may benefit from the extra entropy that port randomization adds.
sections.plainLanguage: A thief needs to know exactly which window to try. Changing the window every time makes the job harder, and it works alongside locks and alarms rather than instead of them.

sections.title: The Update to RFC 5905
sections.content:
The core change replaces the description of the dstport variable in Section 9.1 of RFC 5905. The old text said it was ordinarily port 123. The new text depends on the mode:

  • Broadcast server mode (5) and symmetric modes (1 and 2): it SHOULD contain port 123.
  • Client mode (3): it SHOULD contain a randomized port number, as specified in RFC 6056.

The value becomes the source port of packets sent from that association. The randomized port SHOULD NOT be shared with other associations, so one association does not reveal its port to another.

An implementation may randomize per request or per association. If it randomizes per request, it SHOULD close the socket after each request and response exchange. It MAY wait a period such as 3 seconds for late or duplicate server packets first, so they do not trigger ICMP port unreachable errors at the client.

The RFC adds that most current operating systems already randomize ephemeral ports. A client using POSIX sockets can get this by not calling bind() or by binding to port 0, which means any port.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers that wait for visitors keep their usual door. A client asking for the time picks a random door each time or for each friend, and closes it when done.

sections.title: Effects on Path Selection
sections.content:
Routers using Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) may hash the transport source port to choose a link. So the client port can influence the measured offset and delay.

If the port changes with every request, packets in different exchanges are more likely to take different paths. That can make measurements less stable and hurt clock stability.

Randomizing per association keeps paths steadier, but clients on the same network synchronized to the same server may then show a stable offset between their clocks, because their exchanges consistently take paths with different delay asymmetry. The RFC leaves the per-request or per-association choice to the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: If you take a different road to school every day, some days are slower than others. Keeping to one road makes your trip time steady, but a friend on another road may always arrive at a slightly different time.

sections.title: Traffic Filtering and NAPT Devices
sections.content:
Operators sometimes want to tell NTP requests from NTP responses, for example when mitigating DDoS attacks. If clients use port 123 as their source port, ports alone cannot separate the two. When all clients in a network randomize their ports, requests and responses are easy to tell apart and simple security policies become possible.

Some NAPT devices reportedly do not translate the source port when it is a system port (0-1023). Where such devices are deployed, using port 123 on clients may limit how many hosts can use NTP at the same time. Devices that do translate the port hide the port 123 source from the outside anyway.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone writes the same return address, the post office cannot tell questions from answers. Different return addresses make sorting easy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that NTP has a habit of using common settings even when not strictly necessary, sometimes with negative security and privacy results. Using port 123 for the source and destination port is not required in every mode, and doing so reduces the work an attacker needs for a blind off-path attack.

The issue was assigned CVE-2019-11331 in the U.S. National Vulnerability Database. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Making things easy to guess helps the bad guys, so when a fixed spot is not needed, the clock messages use a random one.
